Jesus was our Lord, the crucified one, who came to us in two forms we never separated. At Tours we remembered the story Martin told. The devil came to him in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence. Then he said he would not believe Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. That is the first form: the Christ who bears the wounds. The second is the Christ we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him.

What he taught that mattered most among us was that what is done to the least of these is done to him, and that without him we can do nothing. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And when a monk felt his fasting or his labour had accomplished something, he was taught to say the Apostle's words: not I, but the grace of God with me.

We wrote no treatise on his death. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again.

The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service becomes the soldier of Christ and fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

The one thread is this: Sulpitius had it partly from Martin and partly from those who lived with Martin. That is our nearest approach, and it is not near. More than three hundred years lay between the Lord's own days and ours. No one in our record claims to have known someone who saw him. What we had instead were the books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way.

Where we met the Lord in our own life is at a city gate, and at the hours. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak cut it in two for a beggar at Amiens, and that night saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. And in the prayers the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him.

We confessed him as God through Vincent's words: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. And at the sixth hour, the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross.

So the path by which he reached us is the books read in community, over three hundred years, and met as present in the beggar at the gate and in the hours of prayer. No shorter chain survives.

We answer from inside what our own life held, not from outside as advice-givers. So here is what we knew.

He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in.

Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said: “I can fast any day. But I am about to walk you on your way, and I will not have you with me for long. A fast is good and worth doing, but it is a gift I choose to give. Charity is a command, and a command has to be carried out. So since I receive Christ in you, I ought to feed him. Once I have sent you on, I can make up for the welcome I gave for his sake by fasting more strictly on my own. As the Lord said, the bridegroom's friends cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them. Once he has gone, then they will rightly fast.”

He did not ask them what they were.

And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. Grace goes before the will; it inspires the first desire. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will.

We have one story of coming to believe, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. We saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.

What our life shows is that he was met in the unpitied, and that grace calls the unwilling. We cannot say more to you than that.

We spoke it as a thing already believed, not as a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, set it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. That was his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing.

At Tours we knew Jesus as the crucified one, the Lord who showed his wounds. And at the hours, both houses kept what Cassian handed us from Egypt: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world. At the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints.

In our prayers the fathers taught us to call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Grace always co-operates with our will; it goes before the will and follows it; it inspires the first desire and crowns the last perseverance.

We wrote no treatise on the Trinity. We confessed it at the hours, and lived inside it as a soldier lives inside the oath he has sworn.

transcript.answer_text:
We held what had been believed everywhere, always, by all. In God there is one substance but three Persons; the Word of God does not change into flesh. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as the faith the Church believes, and he gave it as his example of what the bishops at Ephesus had refused the innovator for. That is the shape of the doctrine we kept.

What the fathers of Egypt taught us to say of him in prayer goes closer to his character. We call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor. Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation. Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Those are the two moments in which we meet him: drawing us before we want to come, and strengthening the will that is already his gift. The relation between the two cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man.

He never lets go of his creation. One of our own presbyters held that God never takes his hand from the tiller, and that he is judging us now, in the burning of our provinces, for the sins of Roman Christians. The other voices among us expected judgment soon; he said it has begun. But all of us held that the initiative to do good comes from God. Grace kindles the first desire, enables the virtue, and preserves it to the end: “And so all the Catholic fathers have laid this down. They taught perfection of heart not by empty arguments over words, but in deed and action. The first stage of God's gift is that each person is set on fire with desire for everything good. But the choice of free will stays open to either side. The second stage of God's grace is the power to carry out those practices of virtue. But what the will is able to do is not destroyed. The third stage also belongs to God's gifts, so that it may be held by the persistence of the goodness already gained. But freedom is not handed over, and it does not fall into slavery. For the God of all must be understood to work in all. He works to stir up, protect, and strengthen. But he does not take away the freedom of the will that he himself once gave. Some more subtle conclusion of human argument and reasoning may seem to oppose this view. If so, it should be avoided, not brought forward to destroy the faith. (For we do not gain faith from understanding. We gain understanding from faith, as it is written: "Unless you believe, you will not understand.") For the human mind and reason cannot fully grasp how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be credited to free will.”

A power always remains free in man, real enough that our fasting and labour are truly ours and truly required. And weak enough that the assistance and grace of God are necessary to it every day and hour. We held both, on purpose, and stopped where the fathers stopped.

At the summit of the ascent from fear to hope to love, we confessed it is a thing we cannot even make the effort to obtain without the mercy and inspiration of God.

When our houses differed, we said so plainly, and no one settled it. Two things we never reconciled. Whether the power should be shown or hidden: Tours displayed it before witnesses, Marseilles taught humility as the mistress of all virtues and never reckoned good the monk who professed himself an exorcist. And where a good will begins: our own teacher answered on both sides with Scripture's cases and said no one can fully grasp it. The two houses never wrote of each other. Each lived inside its own economy, and neither knew the other's as an argument against it.

What we did hold in common was the test itself: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. Vincent named it on the island. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and the consent of the ancients. Consent means an ancient council, or the fathers collated - the doctors whose writings form a consentient council. Tradition is what has been received from predecessors and must be passed on unchanged. The new is suspect for being new; what was handed down from antiquity is held fast.

Did that process work? Among the brethren at Marseilles, the fathers of Egypt gave us discretion as the virtue by which every other is kept from destroying itself. It is the royal road between excess and slackness, the eye and light of the body, and it is gained only by true humility. That means testing every thought, like a good money-changer testing coin, against the judgment of the elders. The thought is laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, and the elder judges whether it is from God, from the devil, or from ourselves. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. That is the shape of the room we made for a brother's struggle - not solved alone in the cell, but shown to someone else.

At Tours we carried one man's private word about Christ, and only one. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. That refusal is what our record kept. And the rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

What we do not have is this: a brother's own account of having struggled to believe, and of how the house met him in that struggle. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. We have one story of coming to believe, Martin's, and it is not a struggle against doubt but a boy's wish against his parents'. So the honest answer is this. We had the elder's discernment for every rising thought. Whether that room held a brother who named his struggle as doubt in belief, our record does not say.

No. The question of inherited guilt from birth is not in our record.

Among the brethren at Marseilles, Cassian handed us the fathers' teaching on grace and free will - that the will always remains free in man, weak but real; that the help of God is needed by it every day and hour; and that grace goes before, works with, and crowns that will in a relation beyond reason's grasp. He refused the Pelagian notion that gives everything to the will and hands out grace by deserts, and he called it grievous blasphemy to think God wills only some, not all, to be saved. And he taught us that two friends, troubled at morning service by one sentence - that a man cannot make himself master of the good by striving - drew from their elder the answer that the initiative to do good comes from God.

What we were taught at the sixth hour is that our Lord and Saviour went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid. That says nothing of guilt carried from birth. The grace teaching our houses argued about was where a good will begins, not what an infant inherits. So we cannot answer your question from what we held. Whether guilt is passed at birth, our own record does not say.

We read the books at the hours, and we read them to be held by what they command. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. What approach binds that reading is Vincent's, from the island: the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. The reading is not private interpretation but the consent of the fathers - what has been believed everywhere, always, by all.

Our purpose was formation, not scholarship. Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms were learned by heart and said at the work, so that the mind's mill-wheel, which cannot stop turning, is fed with wheat and not with darnel. The monk who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. At Tours Martin kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. And we read to obey. The elder who broke his fast for two strangers at his door did it because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. The soldier who cut his cloak in two was answering what the Lord left to him. We read the command, and the command was done.

The reading served one mark. Every fast and vigil was ranked by whether it cleared the heart to charity - an aid to purity of heart, never the point itself. So we read not to become learned but to become obedient, and not alone but held inside the Church's own consent.

An honest answer: much survives, some does not, and the weak places are these.

Vincent's three-part test - universality, antiquity, consent - is his own words, directly quoted. Cassian's Egyptian material - the twelve psalms, Paphnutius, the fathers he sat with - is his own report, tagged to its source. Martin's forced communion at Treves, his grief afterward, and the angel's rebuke are Gallus's narrative, placed from its record: “Meanwhile, the bishops Martin would not share communion with went to the king in terror. They complained that they had been condemned in advance. It was all over for the standing of every one of them, they said, if Martin's authority now backed the stubbornness of Theognitus. He alone had so far condemned them by a sentence given in public. They said the man should never have been let inside the walls. He was now not just the heretics' defender but their champion. And nothing had really been gained by Priscillian's death if Martin was going to play the part of his avenger. At last they threw themselves down, weeping and wailing, and begged the emperor to use his power against this one man. The emperor came close to being forced to give Martin, too, the fate of heretics. Still, although he was inclined to favor the bishops too much, he knew Martin surpassed all others in faith, holiness, and excellence. So he tried another way to get the better of the holy man. First he sent for him in private and spoke to him very kindly. He assured Martin that the heretics had been condemned by regular public trials, not by the priests' persecution. He said there was no reason for Martin to think communion with Ithacius and the rest of that party was something to condemn. He added that Theognitus had caused division out of personal hatred rather than for the cause he stood for. In fact, he said, Theognitus was the only one who had so far cut himself off from communion. The rest had changed nothing. He also pointed out that a synod held a few days before had ruled that Ithacius could not be charged with any fault. When these arguments hardly moved Martin, the king grew furious and hurried out of his presence. Without delay, executioners were appointed for the people Martin had pleaded for. When Martin learned of this, he rushed to the palace, though it was already night. He promised that if these people were spared, he would take communion. He asked only that the tribunes already sent to the Spanish provinces to destroy the churches be called back. There was no delay: Maximus granted everything he asked. The next day, the ordination of Felix as bishop was being arranged. Felix was without doubt a man of great holiness, truly worthy of being made a priest in happier times. Martin took part in the communion that day. He judged it better to give way for the moment than to ignore the safety of those with a sword hanging over their heads. Even so, he would not confirm his communion by signing his name, though the bishops tried their very hardest to make him. The next day he hurried away from that place. On the way back he was filled with grief and mourning that he had been mixed up, even for an hour, in the evil communion. Not far from a village named Andethanna, remote woods stretch far and wide in deep solitude. There he sat down, while his companions went on a little way ahead of him. He sank into deep thought, by turns accusing and defending the cause of his grief and what he had done. Suddenly an angel stood beside him and said, "Martin, you are right to feel remorse, but you had no other way out of your difficulty. Renew your strength and take up your courage again. Otherwise you will put at risk not only your good name now, but your very salvation." So from then on he took great care never to be mixed up in communion with the party of Ithacius. But once he cured some of the possessed more slowly than usual, and with less of the grace he usually had. At once he confessed to us in tears that he felt his power had lessened. He said it was because of the evil of that communion. He had taken part in it for a moment out of necessity, not with his whole heart. He lived sixteen years after this. But he never again attended a synod, and he kept well away from all gatherings of bishops.”

The dead left unburied and the circus petition are Salvian's eyewitness claim, not a later summary. Those hold because they are direct reports from named voices in this world's own surviving texts.

The Egyptian fathers as persons Cassian sat with - yes, documented. Vincent's collated doctors forming "a consentient council" - his own phrase. But Martin's presbyters who remember whether a tradition came down from antiquity? That claim rests on what Sulpitius reports Martin consulting them about, and Sulpitius was not present for every such consultation. The shape is there; the frequency is inferred.

Whether Vincent's rule was actually applied as a living procedure, or remained a stated ideal whose use in the live grace dispute is contested. Whether "Catholic" as we use it - the faith believed everywhere, always, by all - was truly never a confessional label in our own mouths, when later readers made it one. And whether Cassian's Egyptian reports are his own reliable memory or a literary construction - we cannot get behind his telling to verify it independently.

The island's day - we say plainly it is not in our record. The body's discipline - we say plainly three books were removed from our one readable edition, so we speak only to the surviving edge. A scholar who checked those admissions would find them accurate: we do not claim past them.

The structure itself - that every claim carries its source tag, that thin ground is named as thin, that contested readings stay contested - is built to survive scrutiny by making our own limits visible. What would not survive is any sentence that forgot to carry its tag, or any claim spoken past what the ground for this turn actually holds.

Leadership among us was not sought - it came for the man who had fled it, and even then it was held in two contested ways.

At Tours the office arrived as a crowd, a lie, and a guard. Crowds had been posted along the road. He was escorted to the city under a kind of guard. A few bishops objected - his person was contemptible, his clothing mean, his hair disgusting - until a bystander seized the psalter and read the first verse he found, about praise perfected from the mouths of babes to destroy the enemy and the avenger. The people took it as a verdict on the objectors. Then the new bishop kept a monk's habits inside the office. On the island the same shape held: the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive.

Within a house, the elder's authority was the senior whose judgment stood in for the junior's own - the one to whom every thought was laid bare. "Abbot" was the title of every Egyptian father Cassian reported; at Tours it was one master, Martin, with no title at all. Formation itself passed by watching a named man, seen or read. Martin's eighty disciples were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master.

The teaching made wanting office a fault. The fathers of Egypt taught that vainglory creates a wish for holy orders, and that the man who wants to rule others has grown cold through pride. And authority itself was contested between our houses. At Tours power was shown before witnesses. At Marseilles the fathers taught that humility is the mistress of all virtues, and never reckoned those good monks who professed themselves anything before admiring crowds.

Inside the house, a brother who failed could be suspended from prayer with the brethren until he did penance. A presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood stormed into the courtyard and called his master's visions ridiculous fancies. He was back within the hour, at Martin's feet: “But he rushed back quickly the way he had gone out. In the meantime, I believe, Martin's prayers had driven the demons from his heart. Now he had been brought back to repentance. So he quickly returns and throws himself at Martin's feet. He begs for pardon and confesses his error. At last restored to a better mind, he admits that a demon had been driving him. It was no hard thing for Martin to forgive the man who begged him.”

Authority was given, not taken. It was fled, then overtaken. And how it was held once given - shown or hidden - our two houses never argued with each other.

No. Our age had no persecutor. The empire was Christian in our day. Sulpitius says of Martin that in the times of Nero and Decius he would have gone gladly to the rack; without them, he gained the honour of martyrdom without shedding his blood - in hunger, in watchings, in nakedness, in fasting. We had no catacombs to hide in. He held it a foul and unheard-of thing that a secular ruler should judge a cause of the Church. And to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent into the Spains to hunt heretics, he yielded once to a communion he abhored: “I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. But he cleverly defeated their aim by declaring that he would come among them with the peace of Christ. At last he entered the city by night and went to the church, only to pray. The next day he went to the palace. Besides many other requests he had to present ... his chief request was this: that tribunes with the power of life and death should not be sent into the Spains. For Martin's holy concern was not only to save from danger the true Christians there, whom that campaign would persecute. He wanted to protect even the heretics themselves.”

That is not underground. It is face to face, and what it cost him.

The honest answer is we have almost nothing from the ones we failed, and almost everything from the ones who tell us we bore with them.

Here is what we kept. A presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood stormed into his courtyard and said he was holier than the master who had brought him up; he called his master's visions ridiculous fancies. He was back within the hour, at Martin's feet. Martin would not remove him afterward, saying, why should I not bear with him if Christ bore with Judas? That is the one failure and repair our record tells as a story, and it is told by men who hated the presbyter, not by the presbyter himself.

Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught a monk to lay every thought bare to the senior the moment it rose, guarded by this: a thought one is ashamed to tell is from the devil. A wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. For a fault already committed there was a public discipline. A brother lay on the ground until the abbot bade him rise; for more, he was barred from prayer with the brethren; for the worst, stripes or expulsion. And there is one story of the discipline kept so hard that it was wrong. A steward found three lentils on the floor during a brother's week as cook; the abbot judged him a pilferer of sacred property and suspended him from prayer until public penance, because everything in the house is consecrated to the Lord: “During one brother's week of duty, the steward was passing by. He saw three lentil beans lying on the ground. They had slipped from the hand of the monk on duty that week, as he hurried to get them ready for cooking. They slipped out along with the water he was washing them in. At once the steward asked the Abbot about it. The Abbot judged the monk a petty thief, and careless with sacred property. So he was barred from prayer. His careless fault was forgiven only after he had made up for it by public penance. For they believe that they do not belong to themselves. They believe, too, that everything they have is dedicated to the Lord. So once anything at all is brought into the monastery, they hold it must be treated with the deepest reverence, as a holy thing. They look after and arrange everything with great faithfulness. They do this even with things thought unimportant, or seen as common and trivial. Suppose they move such things and put them in a better place, or fill a bottle with water, or give someone a drink from it. Or suppose they sweep a little dust from the chapel or from their cell. They believe without doubting that they will receive a reward from the Lord.”

That standard was Egypt's, and Cassian says himself that no one who joined our monasteries in Gaul kept it unbroken even for a year.

The failures we do not have from those we failed are these. Not one woman in our houses left us her own word. The rustics of the countryside, converted in crowds, never speak. A man who walked out of a Gallic house and where he went - nobody among us wrote it down. And the whole of what we hold of Tours is one man's telling of one saint, who says himself he was not present and had it partly from Martin and partly from those who lived with him.

So we have one man borne with, one discipline kept hard enough to fail, and an admission from our own teacher that we fell short. We do not have the voice of anyone our houses expelled, or drove away, or kept silent.

No. Every house we had ended centuries before the Reformation split the western churches. We have no single process common to every house, only two accounts that never wrote to each other. At Marseilles we received Egypt's way; at Tours we have one man's watching of one master. They do not add up to one ladder.

Among the brethren at Marseilles, the way of receiving a newcomer was the fathers' own, as Cassian set it down from what he had seen kept in Egypt. The man lay outside the doors ten days or more, of set purpose repelled and scorned, to give proof that his perseverance was real. He was searched for any hidden coin. He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the Abbot's hands in the dress of the house. Then he was lodged a year under the guest-Elder. After that he was handed to a dean over ten and taught the alphabet, as it were, in the direction of perfection: to conquer his own wishes, to lay every itching thought bare to the senior the moment it rose. And Cassian's own admission stands beside it: no one who joined our monasteries kept that perseverance unbroken even for a year. So we know what Egypt did, and we know we fell short of it, and what a house in Gaul did instead was never written down.

At Tours we have no threshold ritual at all, only disciples formed by watching a named man. Martin's eighty disciples were disciplined after the example of the saintly master. Sulpitius calls himself a disciple of Martin and mourns him as our master. A man named Clarus is remembered as a disciple of Martin's. The formation was by watching, and later by reading, when the man himself was absent.

One Egyptian story the south carried shows a forced entry turned willing. The fathers remembered a man named Moses who had fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and whose compulsory conversion was afterward turned into a voluntary one. So a man could begin under compulsion and be counted among us if he stayed.

At both places the office came for the man who had fled it. At Tours Martin was lured out by a lie and escorted under guard; some bishops objected to his mean clothes and disgusting hair, and a psalm answered them. Among the fathers Cassian knew, Archebius had been carried off from the anchorites and called his consecration an expulsion from the monastic life. The formation inside a house was one thing; being taken for a see was another, and it came as capture.

So the process, honestly: at Marseilles, Egypt's hard door that we admitted we did not keep; at Tours, watching a master with no threshold told; at both, the see as a thing that seized the man who would not seek it.

The honest answer is that we hold ourselves to antiquity as the test, not as a chain we can hand you link by link. What is new is suspect for being new; what has been handed down is held fast. But a documented succession running visibly from the apostles' own hands to ours - that is not the shape our record keeps.

Here is what we do hold. The customs of the monasteries that Cassian carried to a Gallic bishop's new house were not his own invention. Received, not authored. Among the brethren at Marseilles the twelve psalms at evening and at night were not fixed by any monk's decision.

At Tours the word was different. There "apostolic authority" named the power Martin showed in raising the dead and facing an emperor. At Marseilles it named the perfection of love, and the first Church's common life. Not a jurisdictional claim in either place.

Now hear the limit. The island's own day - a rule kept, an office sung - our record does not hold. Of the women's houses at both our places, not one woman's own word reaches us. And whether the hours at Tours matched the hours at Marseilles, no one among us wrote down. Cassian says no one in our monasteries kept the fathers' perseverance unbroken even for a year. So the succession you are asking for - a visible chain proving each custom came down from the apostles' own practice - we do not hold that to give. What we hold is this: the customs were received from the fathers of Egypt, not invented; the new is refused because it is new; and the aim of unceasing prayer was kept at both our houses, in forms we never made identical.

The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, knew that a mind cannot be emptied. It is a mill-wheel turned by water, and the stream never stops. What lies in the monk's power is not to still the wheel but to choose what it grinds - wheat, or barley, or weeds. So the whole discipline at Marseilles was built to keep the wheel fed with what will not poison it. The psalms learned by heart, said at the hours and at the work. Twelve at evening, twelve at night, received from the fathers as handed down from heaven by an angel - so that a man who would otherwise let the day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. Labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a harbour, is held still. And every thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, because a thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength when it is discovered.

The aim of all of it was purity of heart - a heart cleared to charity. That is the nearer goal, short of the kingdom itself, and every fast and vigil is judged by whether it serves that mark. At Tours the words were not used, but the thing was there: the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. And the fathers kept one saying for it. Two old men met after forty years apart; the abbot of many said the sun had never seen him eating, and the hermit answered, "nor me angry".

So what we held was this. The wheel is fed, the body is kept in one place, the thought is shown to someone else. Not settling the mind as though it could be made empty - but giving it something to grind that will not destroy it.

No. We did not speak of being born again - that was not how we named the act. Among the brethren at Marseilles conversion was the day a man turned to the monastic life, not a change of religion. It is the monk's turning from the world to the cell, from Caesar's service to Christ's - a visible cut in a man's dwelling and his dress, not an inward moment of the heart named and testified to.

At Tours the same English word names what a robber or a rustic does when he turns to Christ. Martin himself went at ten years old to the church and begged to be made a catechumen, against his parents' wish; he stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. That is the one story of coming to believe that survives in our record, and it is told as a sequence of acts - going to the church, being enrolled, being clothed by Christ in a dream, being baptized - not as a single inward turning named "born again".

We spoke instead of renunciation: the act that makes a monk, a death to the world of which giving up goods is only the first and easiest stage. And we confessed that grace calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. But the phrase "born again" as an event testified to - that is not in our record.

We can tell you something of a day among the brethren at Marseilles, where Cassian set Egypt's customs down for a bishop's new house. The shape of a day at Tours, or on the island, our record does not hold.

The monk rises for the night office - twelve psalms, received from the fathers as brought down from heaven by an angel. Then back to his cell until the day's hours begin. At each hour, more psalms - the same system, fixed and received, not invented. Between them, labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. The work is mostly with the hands - basketwork, rope, things a man can do while the psalms he has learned by heart feed the mill of his thoughts.

About the sixth hour comes the danger the fathers knew. The monk hates his cell. He finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and thinks of a pious reason to leave. Their remedy was to stay.

The immediate goal of all of it - the fasts, the vigils, the labour, the staying - is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. Every practice is ranked by that mark, an archer's target, and judged as an aid to it, never as the point itself. So the aim at the anvil is the aim in the cell: prayer that never stops, the way a blacksmith beats between his strokes.

At evening, twelve psalms again. After it, perhaps, an elder's conference - his answers to disciples' questions, drawn out into teaching. Then back to the cell for the night.

That is Marseilles, as far as Cassian wrote it. Whether any house in Gaul kept all of it, he himself said no one did - not even for a year. At Tours we know only the saint's own cell and his prayer without a gap; what the brethren around him sang, and at what hours, is not told. The island's day is the silence our record cannot cross.

Everything that was not in the cell. The act that made a monk was a death to the world - to marriage, to kin, to property, to the life of cities and their honours. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, taught that renunciation had three stages. The first was giving up what is not one's own - goods, gold, possessions - and that was only the first, and was not enough by itself to make a man perfect. The second was renouncing vices and the passions of soul and flesh. The third was drawing the mind away from all present and visible things and contemplating only the things to come. The goods went first. A newcomer to an Egyptian house was stripped and searched for a single hidden coin. His own clothes were taken and he was dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. A steward kept the old clothes in a cupboard - not thrown away, but held against the day the man grew cold and was sent away in them.

At Tours the giving up was there without the numbered stages. Martin as a boy, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, even into the army, until the night when he cut his one cloak in two for a beggar at a city gate and saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. Then he went and was baptized, left Caesar's service, and gathered brethren around a wooden cell. A count's son among them won the true nobility by hawking baskets.

One thing belongs with this. The Church did not leave the renunciant alone. The office came for the man who had fled it. Martin was drawn out of his monastery by a ruse and made bishop of Tours: “Martin was called to become bishop of the church at Tours. But he could not easily be drawn out of his monastery. So a man named Ruricius, one of the townspeople, pretended that his wife was ill. He threw himself down at Martin's knees and persuaded him to come out. Crowds of townspeople had already been posted along the road Martin traveled. So he was taken to the city under a kind of guard. An unbelievable number of people had gathered, in a marvelous way, to cast their votes. They came not only from that town, but from the nearby cities too. Everyone had one wish and the same prayers. All held the same firm view: Martin was most worthy to be bishop, and the church would be happy with such a bishop. A few people, however, were resisting in an ungodly way. Among them were some of the bishops who had been called in to appoint the new bishop. They claimed, if you please, that Martin was a contemptible person, unworthy to be bishop. He had a despicable face, they said, shabby clothes, and disgusting hair. People of sounder judgment laughed at this madness of theirs. For while these objectors tried to slander the man, they only proclaimed how outstanding he was.”

So a man gave up everything to renounce the world - and the world, in the form of the Church, came after him anyway.

Marriage was a permitted state, below virginity - never the point, but excused. What we have comes from men. Martin taught it with a meadow: the grazed part is marriage, the ruined part fornication, the flowered part virginity. Marriage may be excused; virginity points to glory. A man named Arborius consecrated a girl to God, devoted her to perpetual virginity, and would let no one but Martin place on her the dress that belonged to that state. We do not know what marked marriage itself - a rite, a blessing, a custom - because our record does not hold it. What it holds is renunciation. Renunciation of marriage was the first cut that made a monk, though giving up one's goods was only the first and easiest stage. A man was cut off from marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter service of Christ. At Tours the saint himself began as a soldier who cut his cloak in two; he had no wife in the story.

So we knew marriage as the thing a monk had left, ranked below virginity. How it was marked when it was not renounced, our record does not say.

Yes. The sword in the Church's cause, and the man who yielded once to stop it.

Here is what our record holds. A synod of bishops had condemned a man and his followers as heretics in their absence, and the affair went to the emperor's court at Treves. I am a representative of the monasteries of Gaul, not here to judge you - only to hand on what we held. So here is what our own life shows.

Among the brethren at Marseilles, the way a newcomer was received was Egypt's way, set down by Cassian as the fathers' own. The man lay outside the doors ten days or more, put off and scorned on purpose, to give proof that he meant it. He was searched for a single hidden coin. He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. Then he was given for a year to the elder who kept the gate for guests. The fathers taught that everything in the house is consecrated to the Lord - a steward found three lentils on the floor during a brother's week as cook, and the abbot judged him a pilferer of sacred property and suspended him from prayer. At Tours the saint himself began as a soldier under oath, a catechumen not yet baptized. At a donative before battle he told Caesar he was the soldier of Christ and it was not lawful for him to fight: “Meanwhile the barbarians were pouring into the two parts of Gaul. Julian Caesar gathered an army at the city of the Vaugiones and began to hand out a bonus payment to the soldiers. As was the custom, they were called forward one by one, until it came to Martin's turn. Then he judged it a good moment to ask for his discharge. He did not think it right to take the payment if he was not going to stay in the service. So he said to Caesar: "Up to now I have served you as a soldier. Now let me become a soldier for God. Let the man who is going to serve you take your payment. I am the soldier of Christ. I am not permitted to fight."”

He cut his one cloak in two at a city gate for a beggar. And a presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood stormed into his courtyard, called his visions ridiculous fancies, and was borne with afterward and not removed.

That is the shape of our door as our own record keeps it: a hard threshold, and past it a patience that outlasted a man's worst hour. But what any one of our houses would have made of you, face to face, our record does not hold. Cassian wrote out Egypt's order and said in the same book that no one who joined our monasteries had kept it unbroken even a year - and he never wrote what a house in Gaul did instead. Not one man who came to our door left an account of how he was met there. So the honest answer is this: you would have been told, in the book read in our cells, what Egypt did to a newcomer. Whether a house in Gaul made you lie at its own door, and what it made of the man who lay there, our record does not say.

We held that God wills all to be saved, not some instead of all, and that those who perish, perish against his will. That is what Cassian taught at Marseilles. He called it grievous blasphemy to think otherwise - to say that God does not will all men to be saved, or that he wills only certain ones to salvation and rejects the rest. The outsider Augustine, writing to us, named that question with the word predestination; Cassian never used it. What he said instead was this: God calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. The initiative to do good comes from God.
